title: Planetary Geology
subtitle: Read the story written in rocks
description: Learn how scientists use rock shapes, textures and minerals to reconstruct the history of another world.
activity: Compare two rock observations from different missions. What clues might suggest that water changed the rocks? How would you decide which clue is most reliable?
takeaway: Rocks preserve evidence of past environments.

curriculum_alignment.subject: Chemistry
curriculum_alignment.topic: Rocks, minerals and the rock cycle

title: Astrobiology
subtitle: Could another world support life?
description: Astrobiology investigates the origin, evolution and potential for life in the universe. It does not assume life exists wherever water is found.
activity: List two environmental conditions scientists investigate when assessing whether a place could be habitable. For each, explain what measurement or instrument you would use to detect it.
takeaway: Evidence of water can help identify potentially habitable environments, but it is not proof of life.

curriculum_alignment.subject: Biology
curriculum_alignment.topic: Evolution, natural selection and origin of life

title: Seismology & Physics
subtitle: Listen to a world's vibrations
description: Seismometers measure vibrations and seismic waves. Scientists use wave behaviour to infer what lies inside planets and moons. InSight applied this technique on Mars; Apollo applied it on the Moon.
activity: Imagine a wave travels through two different materials — say, solid rock and liquid iron. How might its speed or direction change? Draw a diagram and label the boundary between materials.
takeaway: Waves can reveal information about structures we cannot directly see.

curriculum_alignment.subject: Geography
curriculum_alignment.topic: Earthquakes and tectonic hazards in East Africa

title: Robotics & Engineering
subtitle: Build machines for extreme places
description: Space rovers combine mechanical design, sensors, cameras, power systems and software to operate far from human help. Sojourner proved the concept; Curiosity shows how far it has evolved.
activity: Design a rover feature that would help it cross a rocky surface or communicate with a base station. Identify one engineering trade-off your design requires.
takeaway: Robotics extends human exploration into places that are difficult or dangerous to reach.

title: Chemistry & Mineral Science
subtitle: What are other worlds made of?
description: Instruments such as spectrometers help identify elements and minerals in rocks and soil. Curiosity's ChemCam fires a laser at targets; Sojourner's APXS used X-ray bombardment. Both read what comes back.
activity: Why might identifying a mineral be more informative than simply describing a rock's colour? Describe two minerals found in Uganda and explain what their presence tells you about the environment where they formed.
takeaway: Chemical composition gives clues about how rocks formed and changed.

title: Physics & Measurement
subtitle: Precision, light and forces in space
description: Precise measurement across vast distances requires understanding the speed of light, optics and atomic-precision timing. The Apollo retroreflectors demonstrate how the simplest physics — reflection — can generate 55 years of scientific results.
activity: Calculate the Earth-Moon distance using the speed of light (300,000 km/s) and a round-trip laser time of 2.51 seconds. Then calculate how far the Moon has moved since 1969, given it recedes at 3.8 cm per year.
takeaway: Measurement precision over long timescales reveals changes that are invisible at any single moment.
